lesson.title: Evolution in the Gene Pool: An Introduction to Population Genetics
lesson.summary: Population genetics studies how genetic variation is distributed within a population and how it changes over time, translating the concept of evolution into something precise and measurable at the level of genes.
lesson.body:
Every line of evidence covered so far in this unit, fossils, anatomy, embryology, molecules, biogeography, establishes that evolution has happened and gives clues about how different lineages are related. Population genetics asks a related but different question: given that heritable variation exists within a population right now, recall variation in populations and its role as the raw material natural selection acts on, how do we actually track and measure genetic change as it happens, generation to generation?

The basic unit of study is the population: a group of individuals of the same species living in the same area, capable of interbreeding with each other. All the alleles, the different versions of each gene, carried by all the individuals in that population together make up its gene pool. Population genetics focuses on two related, measurable quantities within that gene pool: allele frequency, how common a particular allele is relative to all versions of that gene in the population, covered in detail in the next chapter, and genotype frequency, how common a particular combination of alleles, like AA, Aa, or aa, is among individuals in the population.

This matters because it turns evolution, often described in introductory terms as change in a species over time, into something with a precise, working definition at the genetic level: evolution is a change in allele frequencies in a population's gene pool from one generation to the next. That definition connects directly back to natural selection. Selection is one of several processes that can change allele frequencies over time, favoring individuals carrying certain alleles so that those alleles become more common in the next generation, but it is not the only one, and part of what population genetics provides is a set of tools for detecting when allele frequencies are changing at all, and, once change is detected, for narrowing down which process is responsible.

The central tool for that detection job is a simple mathematical model called Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, covered after the next chapter on allele frequency. It describes what a population's genotype frequencies would look like if allele frequencies were not changing at all, if the population, in other words, were not evolving. That might sound like an odd thing to build a whole toolkit around, but it turns out to be exactly what is needed. By working out what a genetically static, non-evolving population should look like, biologists get a precise baseline to compare real populations against, and any meaningful difference between the real, observed data and that baseline is a signal that some evolutionary process is actually at work.
